title: Floating-point error in financial analytics
description: A practical counterexample showing how repeated decimal arithmetic creates representation error when financial analytics use binary floating-point numbers.
lead: Financial analytics often repeat simple decimal arithmetic: add ten-cent credits, total transaction fees, compute refund adjustments, or compare calculated amounts to thresholds. The danger is not that every floating-point total becomes visibly wrong. The danger is that decimal business quantities can be represented by nearby binary values, and repeated arithmetic makes that fact observable in totals, comparisons, and reconciliation checks. This guide uses a small hypothetical retail example to demonstrate the representation error directly, without turning the topic into tax, accounting, or rounding policy advice.

sections.heading: The specific problem: repeated decimal values stored as binary floats
paragraphs: A decimal such as 0.10 feels exact because it has a short written form in base ten. A binary floating-point type stores numbers in base two. Fractions whose reduced denominator contains any prime factor other than 2 do not have a finite binary expansion. One tenth is 1 divided by 10, and 10 factors into 2 times 5, so 0.10 cannot be represented exactly as a finite binary fraction.

This matters in financial analytics because many datasets contain repeated decimal quantities: item prices, fees, credits, rates, and per-event adjustments. If those values are stored or computed as binary floating-point values, the analytic total is not the sum of the decimal values users see. It is the sum of nearby binary approximations, plus whatever additional rounding happens during arithmetic.

PostgreSQL’s documentation makes the modeling distinction explicit: numeric can store exact values up to the declared precision, while real and double precision are inexact, variable-precision types. That is the key design issue for analytics. The question is not whether floating point is bad in general. It is whether an inexact binary approximation is acceptable for the specific financial question being answered.

sections.heading: Worked counterexample: a hypothetical ten-cent loyalty credit
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail events table where each qualifying event earns a customer a 0.10 dollar loyalty credit. Suppose an analytics workflow stores that amount in a common binary64 floating-point representation, the format usually meant by double precision floating point in many systems.

In binary64, the decimal value 0.1 is represented by the nearby rational value 3602879701896397 divided by 36028797018963968. That stored value is slightly larger than one tenth. The representation error is not a matter of display formatting; it exists before the value is printed.

The exact error for a single stored 0.10 is calculated as follows. The stored value is 3602879701896397 / 36028797018963968. The intended decimal value is 1 / 10. Subtract the intended value from the stored value:

That is approximately 0.000000000000000005551115123125783 dollars per event. For one event, this is far below a cent. But the important conclusion is not the size; it is the proof that the stored value is not the exact decimal amount.

Now repeat the value. If 100,000 hypothetical events each store this binary approximation of 0.10, then even before considering the rounding performed by each floating-point addition step, the represented values sum to the intended total plus 100,000 times the single-value representation error. The intended decimal total is 10,000.00 dollars. The representation-only excess is approximately 0.0000000000005551115123125783 dollars.

That still does not round to a cent in this example. This is why floating-point errors can be dismissed too casually: a simple total may appear harmless at ordinary display precision. But the counterexample proves a more general rule. A financial pipeline that uses binary floating point for repeated decimal amounts is operating on approximations, not on the decimal business quantities themselves. Whether that difference becomes visible depends on row count, arithmetic sequence, grouping, comparisons, downstream rounding, and tolerance rules.

sections.heading: A comparison counterexample: three tenths are not the same stored value as 0.3
paragraphs: Aggregation is not the only place representation error appears. Equality checks, joins, thresholds, and bucket boundaries can expose it even when totals look normal.

Using the same binary64 representation, the stored value for 0.1 is 3602879701896397 / 36028797018963968. If you take three of those represented one-tenth values and add them as exact rational quantities for demonstration, the result is 10808639105689191 / 36028797018963968.
The nearest binary64 representation of decimal 0.3 is 5404319552844595 / 18014398509481984. With the same denominator as the previous expression, that is 10808639105689190 / 36028797018963968.

Those two quantities differ by 1 / 36028797018963968, approximately 0.000000000000000027755575615628914. In other words, the represented value obtained from three stored tenths is not the same rational value as the stored representation of 0.3.

The practical warning is simple: do not build financial analytics logic that depends on exact equality between binary floating-point results and decimal-looking thresholds. A hypothetical rule such as calculated_credit = 0.30 can be fragile if calculated_credit was produced from repeated floating-point operations. The exact observed behavior depends on the system, expression order, and formatting, but the representation mismatch is enough to justify avoiding exact float equality for money-like quantities.
bullets: Bad pattern: compare a computed floating-point amount directly to a decimal-looking threshold.
Safer pattern: store and compare exact decimal values or integer minor units when the business quantity is money-like.
If a floating-point value is unavoidable for a non-financial analytic measure, compare with an explicit tolerance that is meaningful for that measure, not with exact equality.

sections.heading: A diagnostic for existing analytics schemas
paragraphs: A useful diagnostic is to look for columns whose names imply money, prices, fees, credits, balances, rates, or adjustments while their storage type is binary floating point. This does not prove a bug by itself. It identifies places where a data engineer should ask whether decimal exactness is required.

The following SQL is illustrative for PostgreSQL-style catalogs. It is meant as a schema review query, not as a claim about any specific production system. Column naming conventions vary, so adapt the patterns to the warehouse or application schema being reviewed.

After finding candidate columns, inspect how they are produced and consumed. A float column that stores a machine-learning score is different from a float column that stores a posted transaction amount. The first may be a legitimate approximate measure. The second is likely to create avoidable reconciliation and comparison risk.
bullets: Trace the source: was the value parsed from a decimal text field, computed from other amounts, or loaded from an upstream float?
Trace the consumers: is the column used in financial totals, equality joins, audit extracts, customer-facing reports, or threshold rules?
Trace the arithmetic: is the value repeatedly added, subtracted, multiplied by counts, or grouped across large partitions?
Trace the display: are downstream dashboards hiding extra digits while automated checks use the unrounded stored value?

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL schema review query.
-- Adapt the table schemas and naming patterns before use.
select
    table_schema,
    table_name,
    column_name,
    data_type
from information_schema.columns
where table_schema not in ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
  and data_type in ('real', 'double precision')
  and (
        column_name ~* '(amount|price|fee|cost|credit|debit|balance|refund|tax|rate|revenue)'
      )
order by table_schema, table_name, column_name;

sections.heading: Rules for demonstrating the error without exaggerating it
paragraphs: The goal of a counterexample is to be precise, not dramatic. Floating-point representation error is real, but the right engineering conclusion depends on the quantity and the business use. Use these rules when explaining the issue to analysts, reviewers, or stakeholders.

First, separate representation error from arithmetic-order error. The loyalty credit example above starts with the exact rational value stored for 0.1 and multiplies the single-value error by the number of rows. That isolates the fact that the stored value differs from the intended decimal. Actual floating-point aggregation can add further rounding because each operation is rounded too, and parallel or reordered aggregation can change the sequence of operations.

Second, do not claim that every float total will be wrong by a cent. Many examples remain far below the displayed cent, especially for simple sums. The stronger and more durable claim is that the computation is not exact decimal arithmetic. That is enough to reject binary floating point for values that must reconcile as decimal money.

Third, distinguish money-like facts from approximate analytic measures. A transaction amount, posted fee, invoice balance, or refund amount usually needs exact decimal behavior. A model score, sensor-derived estimate, or exploratory statistic may tolerate approximate floating-point arithmetic. NIST’s discussion of measures of scale is a reminder that analytics often compute derived summaries, not only sums; the required numeric representation should follow the meaning and required tolerance of the measure.

Fourth, prefer explicit modeling choices. For financial facts, common choices are exact decimal types or integer minor units such as cents, depending on the domain. The separate precision-and-scale question is how much capacity to allocate for stored and intermediate values; the point here is narrower: do not accidentally choose binary floating point when the business quantity is decimal and exactness matters.

sections.heading: A practical implementation pattern
paragraphs: For an analytics table that stores financial facts, define the decimal contract close to ingestion and keep it visible. The contract should say which fields are exact amounts, which unit they use, and which fields are approximate measures. That lets reviewers distinguish a deliberate approximate metric from an accidental floating-point money column.

The following illustrative table definition shows the shape of that contract in PostgreSQL. It uses numeric for the exact transaction amount and leaves a separate approximate column for a non-money analytic score. This is not advice about the right precision and scale for every domain; capacity planning for decimal precision is a separate modeling decision.
bullets: Use exact decimal or integer minor-unit storage for posted financial facts.
Avoid exact equality comparisons on computed binary floating-point values.
When reviewing totals, check both storage type and calculation path.
Document any approximate numeric field so future users do not treat it as an exact financial amount.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL table shape for a hypothetical retail order fact.
create table analytics_order_fact (
    order_id bigint primary key,
    customer_id bigint not null,
    order_date date not null,
    posted_amount numeric(18, 2) not null,
    loyalty_credit_amount numeric(18, 2) not null,
    churn_model_score double precision null
);

-- Exact decimal aggregation for money-like fields.
select
    order_date,
    sum(posted_amount) as posted_amount_total,
    sum(loyalty_credit_amount) as loyalty_credit_total
from analytics_order_fact
group by order_date;

takeaways: A short decimal such as 0.10 is not necessarily exact in binary floating point; one tenth has no finite binary expansion.
Repeated decimal arithmetic can expose representation error in totals, equality checks, joins, and thresholds, even when ordinary display formatting hides the difference.
For money-like analytics facts, choose exact decimal or integer minor-unit representations deliberately; reserve binary floating point for approximate measures where that tradeoff is acceptable.

title: Integer overflow in aggregate calculations
description: A practical guide to estimating intermediate numeric bounds for aggregates, so data engineers can size accumulators and aggregate fact tables before overflow appears in production results.
lead: Checking that each input value fits a column type is not enough. Aggregate calculations create larger intermediate values: products before sums, sums before averages, partial totals before final totals, and stored aggregate facts after rollups. The safe question is not only “Can one row fit?” It is “Can the largest plausible intermediate result fit?”

sections.heading: The overflow mistake: validating rows instead of calculations
paragraphs: Integer overflow in aggregate calculations often starts with a true but incomplete statement: every source value fits its declared type. A quantity fits in a small integer. A price in cents fits in a 32-bit integer. A single order line total fits in a 32-bit integer. Then a monthly aggregate, a dashboard rollup, or an aggregate fact table silently exceeds the range of the accumulator or destination column.

The mistake is treating the input range as the calculation range. Aggregates do not preserve the maximum size of their inputs. SUM can grow with row count. AVG may be implemented through a sum and count, so the intermediate sum can be much larger than the final average. Multiplication before aggregation can create a larger term than either operand. Joins can multiply rows before the aggregate sees them. Rollups and cubes intentionally collapse many base facts into fewer, larger facts.

PostgreSQL’s documentation is useful background because it makes type promotion visible. PostgreSQL 18 documents integer ranges for smallint, integer, and bigint, and its aggregate documentation specifies wider return types for some sums, such as sum(integer) returning bigint and sum(bigint) returning numeric. That behavior is protective for those specific PostgreSQL aggregates, but it does not remove the modeling task. Expressions, casts, destination tables, intermediate pipeline steps, other engines, exported files, and aggregate fact tables can still be narrower than the bound required by the calculation.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail counterexample
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order-line dataset that stores prices in cents as integers. This is a numeric representation example, not tax or accounting advice.

Assume the row-level constraints are: quantity is between 0 and 12, unit_price_cents is between 0 and 199,999, and line_gross_cents is computed as quantity times unit_price_cents. The largest row-level line gross is 12 times 199,999, which equals 2,399,988 cents. That fits inside a signed 32-bit integer, whose positive maximum is 2,147,483,647 only if line_gross_cents were smaller; in this case 2,399,988 also fits because it is far below the maximum. The row looks harmless.

Now aggregate by store and month. The maximum number of high-value lines needed to overflow a signed 32-bit sum is small: 894 lines at 2,399,988 cents sum to 2,145,589,272 cents, which is still under 2,147,483,647. The 895th such line produces 2,147,989,260 cents, which exceeds the signed 32-bit maximum by 505,613 cents. Nothing about a single row looked extreme, but the monthly sum crossed the boundary in fewer than 900 maximum-size rows.

The same pattern applies at larger widths. Suppose a different hypothetical aggregate stores a large enterprise amount in cents, with each row bounded at 999,999,999,999 cents. One row fits in signed 64-bit. Ten million such rows sum to 9,999,999,999,990,000,000 cents. That is greater than the signed 64-bit maximum of 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. If the accumulator or destination column is signed 64-bit, the aggregate bound is too large even though every input row fits.

This counterexample is deliberately simple. It leaves out returns, discounts, currency conversion, taxes, and rounding policy because those are separate business rules. The numeric lesson is enough: the aggregate must be sized for row count multiplied by the largest possible term, not for the largest individual input column.

sections.heading: Bound the expression, not just the column
paragraphs: A practical overflow review starts by writing down the expression that the aggregate actually computes. For each grouped metric, identify the term being aggregated, the largest plausible absolute value of that term, and the largest plausible number of rows in one group. If a rollup aggregates already-aggregated data, use the largest plausible number of child groups and the largest child total, not the original row constraint.

For a nonnegative SUM, use this rule: maximum sum equals maximum rows per group times maximum term. If the term can be negative or positive and you need a safe absolute bound, use maximum absolute sum less than or equal to maximum rows per group times maximum absolute term. If positive and negative values can offset each other, do not rely on offsetting for storage safety unless the data model enforces it. Overflow can occur before values cancel, and many partial aggregation plans do not guarantee a helpful order.

For multiplication, bound the product before the sum. If absolute value of a is at most A and absolute value of b is at most B, then absolute value of a times b is at most A times B. For a line amount computed as quantity times unit_price_cents, the term bound is max_quantity times max_unit_price_cents. Then the SUM bound is max_rows_per_group times that product.

For averages, do not stop at the final average range. The final AVG of cents may be within the input range, but the intermediate sum may not be. If the engine computes AVG using a widened accumulator, that may be safe for the aggregate itself; if your pipeline computes sum_cents and count separately, stores sum_cents in an aggregate table, or casts the result, the stored sum still needs its own bound.

For decimal types, think in scaled integer units. If values are stored as dollars with scale 2, the scaled unit is cents. A numeric value with precision p and scale s can store p total significant decimal digits, with s digits after the decimal point. For a SUM stored as numeric(p, s), estimate the maximum absolute scaled integer value and choose p large enough for its digits. For example, if the maximum aggregate is 2,879,985,600,000 cents, that scaled integer has 13 digits, so numeric(13,2) has enough total digits for the cents representation; in practice you may choose a larger precision to allow growth and avoid frequent migrations.
bullets: Write the aggregate expression exactly as computed, including multiplication and casts.
Estimate the maximum absolute value of one aggregate term.
Estimate the maximum rows per group after filters and joins, not just source table size.
Multiply term bound by group row bound for SUM-like metrics.
Compare the result to the accumulator type and the destination column type.

sections.heading: Use post-join grain and aggregate-table grain
paragraphs: The row-count bound must match the grain at the point where the aggregate runs. If a fact table is joined to a dimension with one matching row per key, the row count may be unchanged. If it is joined to a bridge table, a slowly changing dimension without an effective-date filter, or any non-unique lookup, the aggregate may see duplicated facts. Numeric overflow and double counting can arrive together.

A safe bound uses the largest post-join multiplicity. If one order line can match up to 4 campaign rows and the aggregate runs after the join, the row count contribution of that order line is up to 4, not 1. If the metric should not be multiplied, fix the grain before aggregation. If multiplication is intentional, include it in the numeric bound.

Aggregate fact tables and cubes also need separate sizing. Kimball-style aggregate fact tables improve query performance by storing metrics at a higher grain than the base fact table. That higher grain changes numeric ranges. A daily store total, monthly regional total, and all-company yearly total are not the same numeric domain as a single order line. Treat each aggregate table column as a new modeled measurement with its own maximum, precision, and growth assumptions.

sections.heading: A repeatable sizing check
paragraphs: The following illustrative PostgreSQL 18 SQL shows the kind of calculation to keep near a metric definition. It is not presented as executed test evidence. The point is to make the bound review explicit and reproducible in code review. The constants are the hypothetical retail values from above.

This query computes the maximum gross cents for one order line, the maximum aggregate cents for a group, and whether that value would fit in signed 32-bit or signed 64-bit integer ranges. In PostgreSQL specifically, documented aggregate return types may widen some SUM results, but this check is still useful when designing expression casts, exported schemas, and destination aggregate tables.

codeExamples.code:
WITH metric_bounds AS (
  SELECT
    'monthly_store_gross_cents' AS metric_name,
    12::numeric AS max_quantity,
    199999::numeric AS max_unit_price_cents,
    1200000::numeric AS max_rows_per_group
), calculated AS (
  SELECT
    metric_name,
    max_quantity * max_unit_price_cents AS max_term_cents,
    max_rows_per_group * max_quantity * max_unit_price_cents AS max_sum_cents
  FROM metric_bounds
)
SELECT
  metric_name,
  max_term_cents,
  max_sum_cents,
  length(max_sum_cents::text) AS scaled_digits_needed,
  max_sum_cents <= 2147483647::numeric AS fits_signed_int32,
  max_sum_cents <= 9223372036854775807::numeric AS fits_signed_int64
FROM calculated;

sections.heading: Interpreting the example
paragraphs: For the hypothetical monthly store metric, the maximum term is 2,399,988 cents. With 1,200,000 rows in a group, the maximum sum is 2,879,985,600,000 cents. That does not fit signed 32-bit. It does fit signed 64-bit. As a decimal with scale 2, it requires at least 13 total scaled digits to represent the cents value, before adding any safety margin.

The decision is not automatically “use the largest type everywhere.” Wider exact numeric types can have storage and performance tradeoffs, and type behavior varies by system. The engineering decision is to make the bound visible, compare it to the actual accumulator and destination types, and document the assumptions. If the business can plausibly exceed 1,200,000 rows per store-month, increase the row bound. If unit prices or quantities can grow, update the term bound. If a new rollup sums store-months into region-years, calculate a new bound for the new grain.

A useful diagnostic question is: where is the narrowest numeric representation after the expression is introduced? It may be the SQL engine accumulator, a cast in a transformation, a column in an aggregate table, a dataframe type, a message schema, or a BI extract. The calculation is only as safe as its narrowest required representation.

sections.heading: Checklist for aggregate overflow reviews
paragraphs: Use this checklist when adding a metric, changing a grain, or designing an aggregate fact table. It is intentionally mechanical because overflow risk often hides in otherwise ordinary metrics.
bullets: Name the business grain of the output metric, such as store-month, customer-day, or region-year.
Write the exact numeric expression before aggregation.
Convert money-like values to a consistent scaled unit for bound calculations, such as cents, while keeping policy questions separate.
Calculate the maximum absolute term, including products and allowed signs.
Estimate the maximum post-join rows per output group.
Calculate the maximum absolute aggregate and the number of scaled digits required.
Check both the computation type and the stored destination type.
Repeat the check for rollups, cubes, exports, and downstream schemas.
Document whether the bound is a hard constraint, a planning assumption, or a temporary limit.

takeaways: Input column ranges do not prove aggregate safety; SUM, AVG internals, multiplication, joins, and rollups can create larger intermediate values.
Estimate bounds at the expression and grain where the aggregate actually runs: maximum term times maximum post-join rows per group.
Size both the accumulator and the destination schema, especially for aggregate fact tables whose numeric ranges differ from base facts.

title: Unit conversions in analytical models
description: A practical guide to modeling unit conversions so analytical facts keep original units, normalized values, and conversion provenance without corrupting aggregation.
lead: Unit conversion errors rarely announce themselves as data quality failures. More often, they appear as a plausible total that mixes cases, eaches, kilograms, pounds, pallets, liters, or hours as if they were the same thing. The modeling fix is not just to convert everything to one unit. Analytical models should preserve the original measurement, the normalized value used for aggregation, and the provenance of the conversion rule that connected them.

sections.heading: The aggregation problem
paragraphs: A fact table can only support additive quantity analysis when the values being added share the same unit. Summing 10 kilograms and 10 pounds as 20 is not a quantity; it is a formatting accident. The same issue appears in retail order lines, warehouse shipments, usage events, machine telemetry, and subscription entitlements.

The tempting repair is to convert all facts into one reporting unit and drop the original unit. That makes the immediate dashboard easier, but it removes evidence. Analysts can no longer tell whether an order was entered as 2 cases or 24 eaches. Data engineers can no longer prove which conversion factor was used. If the conversion rule changes later, a rebuild may silently change historical quantities.

A safer analytical model separates three ideas: the measurement as received, the normalized measurement used for arithmetic, and the conversion rule used to derive the normalized measurement. This is consistent with a dimensional modeling habit described by Kimball guidance on multiple units of measure: multiple unit representations are a modeling concern, not a presentation afterthought. Kimball’s Type 0 concept is also useful background here: some original descriptive values should be retained rather than overwritten.
This article focuses on numeric representation and aggregation. It does not cover tax treatment, accounting policy, currency conversion dates, or how reversals should affect rate calculations.

sections.heading: Worked hypothetical retail example
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order-line dataset for one product. The product can be ordered as eaches, cases, or pallets. At the time of these orders, 1 case equals 12 eaches and 1 pallet equals 40 cases, so 1 pallet equals 480 eaches.

The source sends these three order lines: line A is 2 cases, line B is 20 eaches, and line C is 0.5 pallets. If a report sums the raw quantity column, it returns 22.5. That number is meaningless because it adds cases, eaches, and pallets.

The correct normalized calculation chooses a base unit, here each, and converts each line before aggregation. Line A is 2 times 12, or 24 eaches. Line B is 20 times 1, or 20 eaches. Line C is 0.5 times 480, or 240 eaches. The additive total is 284 eaches.

Now consider a counterexample. Suppose the current product master later says that a case contains 10 eaches and a pallet contains 40 of those new cases. If historical facts only store original_quantity and original_uom, and reports join to the current product master for conversion, the same three historical lines recalculate as 20 eaches, 20 eaches, and 200 eaches. The reported historical total becomes 240 eaches instead of 284. Nothing in the report looks technically broken; it is just wrong by 44 eaches.

The lesson is not that conversion rules can never change. The lesson is that the fact must preserve the conversion rule that was used, or enough immutable inputs to reconstruct it. The normalized value is for aggregation. The original value is for auditability and user explanation. The conversion provenance is for reproducibility.
bullets: Naive raw sum: 2 plus 20 plus 0.5 equals 22.5, which has no interpretable unit.
Correct historical normalized sum: 24 plus 20 plus 240 equals 284 eaches.
Incorrect recomputation with current rules: 20 plus 20 plus 200 equals 240 eaches.

sections.heading: Minimum columns to store
paragraphs: A practical unit-aware fact table does not need to become complicated, but it does need explicit columns. At minimum, store the original quantity, original unit, normalized quantity, normalized unit, and conversion provenance. Avoid binary floating-point types for business quantities that need repeatable decimal arithmetic. Use fixed-precision decimal types or exact integer numerator and denominator factors where possible.

For ratio conversions, a useful formula is: base_quantity equals original_quantity multiplied by conversion_factor_numerator divided by conversion_factor_denominator. This covers cases such as pounds to ounces, cases to eaches, or hours to minutes. It does not cover every possible measurement transformation. Temperature conversions, for example, include an offset and should not be forced into a pure multiplier model.

The base unit should be chosen per additive measure, not globally for the warehouse. Units sold might use eaches. Weight might use grams or kilograms. Volume might use milliliters or liters. Duration might use seconds. The important rule is that a single additive metric should aggregate on one base unit.

The conversion rule should be identifiable and stable. A rule identifier lets downstream users trace the normalized value back to a reference row. Denormalized copies of the numerator, denominator, source system, and effective timestamp make the fact resilient if the reference table is later corrected, retired, or reloaded. In high-control environments, the conversion rule table itself should be append-only or otherwise versioned.
bullets: original_quantity: the number as received from the source event or transaction.
original_uom_code: the unit as received, such as case, each, lb, kg, or pallet.
base_quantity: the normalized value used for additive analysis.
base_uom_code: the unit of base_quantity, such as each or gram.
conversion_rule_id: an identifier for the rule used at load time.
conversion_factor_numerator and conversion_factor_denominator: exact ratio inputs when a ratio conversion is valid.
conversion_applied_at: when the analytical pipeline applied the conversion.
conversion_source: where the rule came from, such as product master, supplier feed, standards table, or manual stewardship table.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative SQL. Adapt data types, constraints, and syntax to your warehouse.
CREATE TABLE conversion_rule (
  conversion_rule_id        VARCHAR(100) PRIMARY KEY,
  from_uom_code             VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  to_uom_code               VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  factor_numerator          DECIMAL(38, 12) NOT NULL,
  factor_denominator        DECIMAL(38, 12) NOT NULL,
  effective_from_date       DATE NOT NULL,
  effective_to_date         DATE,
  conversion_source         VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE fact_order_line_quantity (
  order_line_id             VARCHAR(100) PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id                  VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  product_id                VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  order_date                DATE NOT NULL,
  original_quantity         DECIMAL(38, 12) NOT NULL,
  original_uom_code         VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  base_quantity             DECIMAL(38, 12) NOT NULL,
  base_uom_code             VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  conversion_rule_id        VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  conversion_factor_num     DECIMAL(38, 12) NOT NULL,
  conversion_factor_den     DECIMAL(38, 12) NOT NULL,
  conversion_applied_at     TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  conversion_source         VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

sections.heading: Explicit calculation rules
paragraphs: Unit conversion logic should be written as calculation rules, not left as tribal knowledge inside transformation code. The rules below are intentionally narrow. They are designed for additive analytical facts where ratio conversion is valid.

Rule 1: never aggregate original_quantity across more than one unit. It is acceptable to show original quantities grouped by original unit, such as 2 cases and 20 eaches. It is not acceptable to sum them into one total without conversion.

Rule 2: aggregate base_quantity only when base_uom_code is the same. A model can contain multiple base units for different measures, but a single measure total should have one base unit. If a query returns more than one base unit for the same additive metric, the result should be treated as invalid until the grouping or filter is corrected.

Rule 3: do not recompute historical base_quantity from a current dimension unless the metric definition explicitly says to restate history. Most operational analytics should report the value derived from the rule in effect for the fact. If restatement is required, model it as a separate derived dataset or versioned metric, not as an invisible change to the original fact.

Rule 4: preserve enough provenance to answer three questions: what was received, what was reported, and why. For a quantity fact, those answers are original_quantity with original_uom_code, base_quantity with base_uom_code, and conversion_rule_id with factor inputs and source metadata.

Rule 5: round at declared boundaries, not at every intermediate step. For example, keep line-level base quantities at sufficient decimal precision and round only for presentation or for a published metric definition. Repeated rounding can create small but avoidable discrepancies when line-level results are summed.

Rule 6: use weighted calculations when deriving averages over converted quantities. If average case size, average shipment weight, or average usage per event is needed, define the numerator and denominator explicitly after normalization. A simple average of already-rounded display values can differ from a calculation over the underlying base quantities.

codeExamples.code:
-- Diagnostic: detect whether one additive metric contains multiple base units.
SELECT
  base_uom_code,
  COUNT(*) AS row_count,
  SUM(base_quantity) AS total_base_quantity
FROM fact_order_line_quantity
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
  AND order_date < DATE '2026-02-01'
GROUP BY base_uom_code;

-- If this returns more than one base_uom_code for a metric that is supposed
-- to be additive in a single unit, stop and inspect the model or filters.

sections.heading: Diagnostics for existing models
paragraphs: If an existing warehouse already has unit-bearing facts, the first diagnostic is simple: find every quantity column that lacks an adjacent unit column. A column named quantity, weight, volume, duration, or amount should raise a question. The unit may be implicit in documentation, but implicit units are fragile because queries cannot validate them.

The second diagnostic is to group by unit before summing. If a report currently returns total quantity, rerun the query grouped by original unit and base unit. If the raw quantity total changes interpretation depending on the group-by columns, the model is mixing measurements.

The third diagnostic is conversion drift. Compare stored base quantities with values recomputed from the current conversion table. Differences are not automatically errors; they may show that the historical fact correctly preserved an older rule. But unexplained differences identify facts that need lineage review.

The fourth diagnostic is precision loss. Look for integer casts, binary floating-point columns, early rounding, or text-formatted numbers in transformation steps. A model can preserve the right unit and still lose numeric correctness if it stores a repeating decimal conversion in insufficient precision. This is especially important when facts are later aggregated across millions of rows.

The fifth diagnostic is report behavior. A good semantic layer should make the safe path easy: expose base_quantity for additive totals, display original_quantity only with original_uom_code, and keep conversion provenance available for drill-through. Hiding original units may make the dashboard cleaner, but it weakens the ability to explain numbers when users challenge them.

codeExamples.code:
-- Diagnostic: compare stored historical conversions to a current rule table.
-- Differences may be legitimate, but they should be explainable.
SELECT
  f.order_line_id,
  f.original_quantity,
  f.original_uom_code,
  f.base_quantity AS stored_base_quantity,
  (f.original_quantity * c.factor_numerator / c.factor_denominator) AS recomputed_base_quantity,
  f.conversion_rule_id AS stored_rule_id,
  c.conversion_rule_id AS current_rule_id
FROM fact_order_line_quantity f
JOIN conversion_rule c
  ON f.original_uom_code = c.from_uom_code
 AND f.base_uom_code = c.to_uom_code
 AND c.effective_to_date IS NULL
WHERE f.base_quantity <> (f.original_quantity * c.factor_numerator / c.factor_denominator);

sections.heading: Modeling tradeoffs
paragraphs: There is a storage cost to keeping original values and conversion provenance. In most analytical systems, the extra columns are small compared with the cost of ambiguous metrics. The bigger tradeoff is cognitive: modelers must decide which unit is canonical for each measure, where conversion rules live, and when historical values may be restated.

Do not solve that tradeoff by storing only every possible converted unit as separate facts. A few high-value alternate units can be useful, especially when users regularly need both eaches and cases. But an uncontrolled set of converted columns creates its own ambiguity. The safer core is one original measurement, one declared base measurement, and traceable conversion metadata.

Also avoid pushing all conversion to the BI layer. Presentation tools can format units, but additive correctness belongs upstream in the analytical model. If every dashboard author chooses conversion logic independently, totals will diverge. Centralizing conversion in the model gives reports a common arithmetic foundation while still preserving the original source measurement.

Finally, be explicit about non-convertible or conditionally convertible values. If a product’s case size is unknown, do not invent a factor just to keep the pipeline green. Mark the conversion status, quarantine the affected fact from additive totals, or publish it only in grouped original-unit form until the rule is supplied. A missing conversion is a data quality issue; a guessed conversion is a metric correctness issue.

takeaways: Store original quantity and original unit beside the normalized quantity. The original measurement is evidence, not clutter.
Aggregate only normalized values that share the same base unit. Raw quantities with mixed units should be grouped by unit or rejected for additive totals.
Keep conversion provenance on or near the fact: rule id, factor inputs, source, and applied timestamp. This prevents historical results from being silently rewritten by current reference data.
Use fixed-precision decimal or exact ratio inputs for repeatable analytical arithmetic; avoid unnecessary floating-point and premature rounding.
Treat missing or changing conversion rules as modeling decisions that require explicit status, versioning, and metric definitions.

title: Exchange-rate direction and inversion
description: A practical guide to modeling exchange-rate direction so currency normalization uses the right multiplication or division rule.
lead: Currency conversion bugs often come from a small ambiguity: does the stored rate mean source per target, target per source, or merely “the rate between two currencies”? The arithmetic is simple, but only if the rate direction is part of the data contract. This guide gives data engineers an explicit rule, a numeric counterexample, and a small modeling pattern for preventing multiplication-versus-division errors in currency normalization.

sections.heading: The problem is not the formula
paragraphs: Most exchange-rate mistakes in analytics are not caused by a difficult formula. They are caused by an underspecified rate. A value of 1.25 between EUR and USD is meaningless until the model says whether it means 1 EUR equals 1.25 USD or 1 USD equals 1.25 EUR. Once the direction is clear, the operation is mechanical.

A robust currency model should make this sentence true for every stored rate: 1 unit of base_currency equals rate units of counter_currency. With that contract, converting from base to counter uses multiplication, and converting from counter to base uses division. If the model instead stores from_currency, to_currency, and rate_to_currency, the equivalent contract is: 1 unit of from_currency equals rate units of to_currency, and normalization to to_currency uses multiplication. Either pattern can work. The unsafe pattern is storing currency_a, currency_b, and rate without a directional meaning.

The article is limited to numeric correctness in normalization. It does not decide which business date should be used for conversion, whether tax should be included, or how accounting policy should define recognized revenue. Those are separate business rules. The goal here is narrower: prevent a pipeline from turning the right source amount into the wrong normalized amount because the engineer multiplied when the data contract required division, or divided when it required multiplication.
bullets: Directional contract: 1 base_currency = rate counter_currency.
Base to counter: amount_counter = amount_base × rate.
Counter to base: amount_base = amount_counter ÷ rate.
Identity conversion: if source currency already equals target currency, keep the amount unchanged.

sections.heading: A hypothetical counterexample
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail-order dataset. The reporting target is USD. The exchange-rate table stores a directional quote: base_currency, counter_currency, and rate, where 1 base equals rate counter. The rates used in this example are intentionally simple so the arithmetic can be checked by inspection.

The rate EUR/USD = 1.25 means 1 EUR equals 1.25 USD. A 100.00 EUR order normalized to USD is therefore 100.00 × 1.25 = 125.00 USD. Dividing instead gives 80.00 USD, which is plausible-looking but wrong under this contract. That plausibility is why inversion bugs can survive ordinary dashboard review: the number is not null, not negative, and often not obviously impossible.

The rate USD/JPY = 110.00 means 1 USD equals 110 JPY. A 11000 JPY order normalized to USD travels in the reverse direction of the stored quote. The correct operation is 11000 ÷ 110 = 100 USD. Multiplying would produce 1210000 USD, which is obviously wrong in this small example. In real data, the wrong operation may not always be that visible because amounts, rate magnitudes, and report filters vary.

Using four hypothetical orders, the correct total is easy to verify: 100 EUR becomes 125 USD, 80 USD remains 80 USD, 11000 JPY becomes 100 USD, and 50 GBP at GBP/USD = 1.60 becomes 80 USD. The normalized total is 125 + 80 + 100 + 80 = 385 USD. An unsafe “always multiply by the joined rate” implementation would produce 125 + 80 + 1210000 + 80 = 1210285 USD because it treats the JPY order as though the stored quote were JPY/USD rather than USD/JPY.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative SQL only. The arithmetic follows the stated directional contract:
-- 1 base_currency = rate counter_currency.

WITH orders AS (
  SELECT * FROM (VALUES
    (1, 'EUR', CAST(100.00 AS numeric(18,2))),
    (2, 'USD', CAST(80.00  AS numeric(18,2))),
    (3, 'JPY', CAST(11000.00 AS numeric(18,2))),
    (4, 'GBP', CAST(50.00  AS numeric(18,2)))
  ) AS t(order_id, currency_code, amount)
),
fx_rates AS (
  SELECT * FROM (VALUES
    ('EUR', 'USD', CAST(1.250000000 AS numeric(18,9))),
    ('GBP', 'USD', CAST(1.600000000 AS numeric(18,9))),
    ('USD', 'JPY', CAST(110.000000000 AS numeric(18,9)))
  ) AS t(base_currency, counter_currency, rate)
)
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  o.currency_code,
  o.amount,
  CASE
    WHEN o.currency_code = 'USD' THEN o.amount
    WHEN o.currency_code = r.base_currency AND r.counter_currency = 'USD'
      THEN o.amount * r.rate
    WHEN o.currency_code = r.counter_currency AND r.base_currency = 'USD'
      THEN o.amount / r.rate
  END AS amount_usd,
  CASE
    WHEN o.currency_code = 'USD' THEN 'identity'
    WHEN o.currency_code = r.base_currency AND r.counter_currency = 'USD' THEN 'multiply'
    WHEN o.currency_code = r.counter_currency AND r.base_currency = 'USD' THEN 'divide'
  END AS operation_used
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN fx_rates r
  ON (
    (o.currency_code = r.base_currency AND r.counter_currency = 'USD')
    OR
    (o.currency_code = r.counter_currency AND r.base_currency = 'USD')
  );

sections.heading: Model rates as directed facts
paragraphs: The safest data model is one where the direction is impossible to ignore. A table named fx_rates with columns base_currency, counter_currency, and rate is better than a table with currency_1, currency_2, and rate. The names encode the contract. If a downstream model wants a universal multiplication rule, create a derived table with from_currency, to_currency, and rate_to_currency, where every row is oriented toward the desired target or all needed directed pairs are generated explicitly.

There is a tradeoff. Keeping only one canonical quote avoids duplicate inverse rows that can drift apart. It also forces conversion code to handle both multiplication and division. Generating both directions makes downstream joins easier because amount_to = amount_from × rate can be the only calculation rule, but it introduces a maintenance risk: if EUR/USD is stored as 1.25 and USD/EUR is separately stored as 0.79, the two rows disagree. If inverse rows are materialized for convenience, they should be derived from a canonical source, not manually maintained as independent facts.

Dimensional modeling guidance from Kimball treats multiple currencies as a modeling concern rather than a formatting afterthought: transaction facts can carry local currency amounts and standardized currency amounts, with exchange-rate handling made explicit. That advice is compatible with the rule here. Whether the normalized amount is stored in a fact table or calculated in a semantic layer, the exchange-rate direction should be a declared part of the schema, not hidden in tribal knowledge.

Numeric representation matters too. PostgreSQL documents numeric as an exact, user-specified precision type and describes it as suitable where exactness is required, including monetary amounts. That does not make every financial model correct, but it avoids introducing binary floating-point representation error into the conversion step. A common pattern is to store source amounts and rates as fixed-precision numeric values, calculate normalized amounts with sufficient intermediate scale, and round only at the boundary required by the consuming business rule.
bullets: Use descriptive directional column names: base_currency and counter_currency, or from_currency and to_currency.
Add constraints such as rate > 0 and base_currency <> counter_currency.
Prefer one canonical quote plus generated inverses over independently maintained inverse rows.
Store the operation used or the directed rate identifier when traceability matters.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative schema fragment for a canonical directed-rate table.
-- Precision and scale should be selected for the currencies and feeds in use.

CREATE TABLE fx_rate_quote (
  rate_date date NOT NULL,
  base_currency char(3) NOT NULL,
  counter_currency char(3) NOT NULL,
  rate numeric(20,10) NOT NULL,
  source_system text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (rate_date, base_currency, counter_currency, source_system),
  CHECK (base_currency <> counter_currency),
  CHECK (rate > 0)
);

-- Optional derived orientation for a target currency, shown for USD.
-- Rows emitted by this view all mean: 1 from_currency = rate_to_usd USD.

CREATE VIEW fx_rate_to_usd AS
SELECT
  rate_date,
  base_currency AS from_currency,
  rate AS rate_to_usd,
  'multiply canonical quote' AS derivation
FROM fx_rate_quote
WHERE counter_currency = 'USD'

UNION ALL

SELECT
  rate_date,
  counter_currency AS from_currency,
  1 / rate AS rate_to_usd,
  'inverse of canonical quote' AS derivation
FROM fx_rate_quote
WHERE base_currency = 'USD'

UNION ALL

SELECT
  rate_date,
  'USD' AS from_currency,
  CAST(1 AS numeric(20,10)) AS rate_to_usd,
  'identity' AS derivation;

sections.heading: Diagnostics that catch inversion
paragraphs: A useful diagnostic checks whether the pipeline can explain the operation used for every converted row. A normalized fact should not merely contain amount_usd. It should be possible to trace that amount to a rate row and an operation: identity, multiply, or divide. If a row has a non-target source currency and no operation, it is not safely normalized. If a row has an operation that conflicts with the rate direction, the model should fail before it reaches a dashboard.

Another diagnostic compares aggregate behavior against expected bounds. For a small controlled fixture, the expected total can be written down before implementation. In the hypothetical example above, the USD total must be 385. If a query produces 180, it probably divided the EUR amount by 1.25. If it produces 1210285, it probably multiplied JPY by a USD/JPY quote while trying to normalize JPY to USD. These are not statistical tests; they are deterministic contract tests.

If both quote directions are stored, an inverse-consistency check can detect drift. For a pair such as EUR/USD and USD/EUR on the same date and from the same source, the product of the two rates should be close to 1, allowing for rounding. For example, if EUR/USD is 1.25, the exact inverse is 0.8. A stored inverse of 0.79 gives 1.25 × 0.79 = 0.9875, which is not just a different presentation; it changes normalized amounts. The acceptable tolerance depends on the precision and source feed, but the invariant itself is simple: a rate and its inverse cannot both be arbitrary.

Error handling should preserve evidence. Kimball’s error event schema pattern is relevant here because rejected or suspicious records deserve a queryable place to land. If a conversion row is missing a rate, has multiple candidate rates under the same business key, or violates inverse consistency, the pipeline should produce an error event with the relevant keys and reason. That is more useful than silently defaulting to 1, dropping the row, or emitting a null that later becomes zero in an aggregate.
bullets: For each converted row, record or derive the operation used.
Use a tiny deterministic fixture with known totals as a regression test.
Check inverse pairs with a tolerance if both directions are stored.
Send missing, ambiguous, or inconsistent rate matches to an error-event path rather than hiding them.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative inverse-consistency diagnostic for tables that store both directions.
-- The tolerance here is an example; choose one based on source precision and rounding policy.

SELECT
  a.rate_date,
  a.base_currency,
  a.counter_currency,
  a.rate AS forward_rate,
  b.rate AS inverse_rate,
  (a.rate * b.rate) AS product
FROM fx_rate_quote a
JOIN fx_rate_quote b
  ON a.rate_date = b.rate_date
 AND a.base_currency = b.counter_currency
 AND a.counter_currency = b.base_currency
 AND a.source_system = b.source_system
WHERE a.base_currency < a.counter_currency
  AND ABS((a.rate * b.rate) - 1) > CAST(0.000001 AS numeric(20,10));

sections.heading: Aggregation rules after conversion
paragraphs: Currency normalization should happen at the row grain where the source amount, source currency, target currency, and selected rate are all known. Then the normalized amounts can be summed. Summing local-currency amounts across currencies before conversion is not meaningful: 100 EUR plus 11000 JPY is not 11100 of any one currency. Averaging rates and applying the average to a mixed-currency total is also unsafe because rates are directional and amounts have different weights.

If an aggregate implied rate is needed for reconciliation, calculate it from already aligned quantities: sum(normalized_target_amount) divided by sum(source_amount) for a single source currency and a single target currency under a consistent direction. Do not average EUR/USD, GBP/USD, and USD/JPY together and call the result a portfolio rate. The units differ. EUR/USD is USD per EUR, GBP/USD is USD per GBP, and USD/JPY is JPY per USD. The labels are part of the math.

Rounding should be delayed until the model boundary where a rounded value is required. For example, a reporting table might keep amount_usd_unrounded for reconciliation and amount_usd_rounded for display. The exact names are less important than making the rounding step explicit. Direction errors are much larger than rounding differences, but hidden rounding can make reconciliation harder when diagnosing an inversion bug.

takeaways: Never store an exchange rate without its direction. A value is not enough; the model must say what one unit of which currency equals.
Use a simple rule: base to counter multiplies, counter to base divides. If you want universal multiplication, generate a directed from_currency-to_currency rate table.
Validate with deterministic fixtures and diagnostics. Known totals, operation labels, and inverse-consistency checks catch many multiplication-versus-division errors before they reach reports.
Convert at the transaction or fact grain before aggregating. Mixed local-currency totals and averaged cross-currency rates are unit errors, not shortcuts.

title: Geometric means for compounded growth
description: A practical guide for identifying when arithmetic averages misstate cumulative change, with checked counterexamples and SQL-style calculation rules for compounded growth rates.
lead: Arithmetic averages answer an additive question: what is the typical value of these observations? Compounded growth asks a multiplicative question: what constant rate would produce the same start-to-end change? Those are not interchangeable. When a metric moves by successive percentages, averaging the percentages can report stable growth even when the underlying count fell. The geometric mean is the usual tool for summarizing a sequence of positive multiplicative factors, but it is also easy to misuse. The practical skill is knowing when the data generating process is multiplicative, when a weighted arithmetic average is the right answer instead, and when the input values are invalid for a geometric calculation.

sections.heading: Why arithmetic averages fail for compounding
paragraphs: An arithmetic mean preserves sums. If four daily order counts are 100, 120, 80, and 140, their arithmetic mean is 110 because the four values sum to 440. That is the right calculation for a typical daily count, assuming each day has equal weight.

Compounded growth does not add rates; it multiplies growth factors. A 20% increase is a factor of 1.20. A 10% decrease is a factor of 0.90. If those happen in sequence, the combined factor is 1.20 times 0.90, or 1.08. The cumulative change is 8%, not the arithmetic average of 20% and negative 10%.

The geometric mean answers a different question: what constant per-period factor would produce the same cumulative factor over the same number of periods? For growth rates r1 through rn, first convert each rate to a factor fi = 1 + ri. The cumulative factor is the product of the factors. The geometric mean factor is the nth root of that product. The geometric mean growth rate is that factor minus 1.

This distinction matters in data modeling because many warehouse tables store monthly growth rates, retention changes, price index changes, or portfolio-like return series as percentages. Those percentages look averageable. But if a downstream dashboard uses their arithmetic mean as average monthly growth, it may no longer reconcile to the start and end values.
bullets: Use an arithmetic mean when the business question is additive: average order value, average shipment weight, average daily tickets, or average revenue per customer for a fixed grain.
Use a weighted arithmetic mean when combining rates across entities in the same period: total conversions divided by total visitors, not the simple average of store-level conversion rates.
Use a geometric mean when the rates are sequential changes on the same base, or on an index intended to chain through time.
Do not use a geometric mean when the multiplicative factor is negative. For ordinary nonnegative business quantities, a rate below negative 100% is invalid rather than merely inconvenient.

sections.heading: Worked example: a hypothetical retail customer count
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail dataset that tracks active customers at month end. The starting count is 10,000. Four monthly growth rates are recorded as 20%, negative 10%, 15%, and negative 25%. These are sequential changes on the same metric, so the compounding question is multiplicative.

Convert each percentage change to a factor: 1.20, 0.90, 1.15, and 0.75. The cumulative factor is 1.20 times 0.90 times 1.15 times 0.75, which equals 0.9315. The ending count implied by the sequence is 10,000 times 0.9315, or 9,315 customers. The cumulative change is therefore negative 6.85%.

The arithmetic mean of the four monthly rates is 0%: (20% minus 10% plus 15% minus 25%) divided by 4 equals 0%. If that average is interpreted as average monthly compounded growth, it says the constant-rate path is flat and would end at 10,000 customers. That is wrong by 685 customers in this example.

The geometric mean fixes the reconciliation problem. The geometric mean factor is the fourth root of 0.9315, approximately 0.982416. The corresponding monthly growth rate is approximately negative 1.7584%. Applying that same monthly rate for four months gives the original cumulative factor: 0.982416 to the fourth power is approximately 0.9315, and 10,000 times 0.9315 is 9,315.

This does not mean the business literally lost 1.7584% of customers every month. It means that negative 1.7584% is the constant monthly rate equivalent to the observed four-month path. The geometric mean is a reconciliation statistic, not a replacement for the actual month-by-month history.

codeExamples.code:
Hypothetical monthly customer growth

Start active customers: 10,000
Monthly rates: +20%, -10%, +15%, -25%
Factors: 1.20, 0.90, 1.15, 0.75

Cumulative factor = 1.20 * 0.90 * 1.15 * 0.75 = 0.9315
Ending customers = 10,000 * 0.9315 = 9,315
Cumulative change = 0.9315 - 1 = -0.0685 = -6.85%

Arithmetic mean rate = (0.20 - 0.10 + 0.15 - 0.25) / 4 = 0.00 = 0%
Geometric mean rate = 0.9315^(1/4) - 1 ≈ -0.017584 = -1.7584%

sections.heading: Counterexamples that expose the error
paragraphs: A compact diagnostic counterexample is a 100% gain followed by a 50% loss. The arithmetic mean rate is 25% because (100% minus 50%) divided by 2 equals 25%. But the factors are 2.00 and 0.50, whose product is 1.00. The start and end values are identical. The equivalent compounded growth rate is 0%, not 25%.

Another useful counterexample is the reverse: a 50% loss followed by a 100% gain. The arithmetic mean is still 25%, the product is still 1.00, and the geometric mean rate is still 0%. Compounding is path-order independent for the final product when the same factors are used, but the arithmetic mean still gives the wrong compounded interpretation.

There is also a boundary case: a 100% loss. If an active-customer segment goes from 1,000 to 0 in one period, the factor is 0. Any later percentage increase from zero is not defined against the same base in the ordinary way. For a finite sequence that includes a factor of zero, the cumulative product is zero and the equivalent rate over the full sequence is negative 100%. Taking logarithms of zero is not allowed, so SQL implementations that use log sums must handle this case explicitly.

Finally, there are cases where a geometric mean is the wrong repair. Suppose a hypothetical retailer has two stores in the same month. Store A has 1 purchase from 10 visits, a 10% conversion rate. Store B has 90 purchases from 100 visits, a 90% conversion rate. The simple arithmetic average of the two store rates is 50%, but the companywide conversion rate is 91 purchases divided by 110 visits, or about 82.73%. The issue here is denominator weighting, not compounding. A geometric mean would not answer the companywide conversion question either.
bullets: If the rates describe sequential changes through time, test whether multiplying factors is the natural reconstruction of the end value.
If the rates describe parallel groups in the same period, inspect the denominator and use an appropriate weighted arithmetic calculation.
If the rate is below negative 100%, treat the record as invalid for ordinary compounded growth on a nonnegative quantity.
If the rate is exactly negative 100%, handle the zero factor as a special case instead of passing it into a logarithm.

sections.heading: Calculation rules for data models
paragraphs: A reliable data model should make the grain and the reconstruction rule explicit. For compounded growth, store enough information to recover the ordered sequence: entity, period, starting value or prior value, ending value, and the calculated factor or rate. Storing only a pre-averaged percentage removes the evidence needed to choose the right aggregation later.

The safest conceptual formula is product(factor) minus 1 for cumulative growth, and product(factor) raised to 1 divided by n, minus 1, for the equivalent per-period growth rate. In analytical SQL, the product is often computed through a sum of logarithms: exp(sum(ln(factor))). This is convenient because many SQL engines have sum and average aggregate functions, but it requires positive factors. Zero and negative factors must be validated before the logarithm step.

The following is illustrative PostgreSQL-style SQL, aligned with PostgreSQL 18 documentation for aggregate functions such as avg, sum, and count. It is not execution evidence and should be adapted to the exact SQL engine, data types, and version in use. The input column period_rate is assumed to store decimal rates, so 0.20 means 20% and negative 0.10 means negative 10%.

The query returns both the arithmetic mean and the compounded calculations so reviewers can see the discrepancy. It also exposes invalid rates below negative 100% and treats an exact negative 100% as a zero cumulative factor. For production models, prefer deriving period_rate from auditable starting and ending values where possible, then applying checks at the semantic model or transformation layer.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL-style SQL, not execution evidence.
-- Assumptions:
--   period_rate is a decimal rate: 0.20 = +20%, -0.10 = -10%.
--   One row represents one period in the sequence for a segment.
--   Rates below -1.0 are invalid for nonnegative compounded quantities.

WITH monthly_growth(segment, period_number, period_rate) AS (
  VALUES
    ('hypothetical-retail-active-customers', 1,  0.20::numeric),
    ('hypothetical-retail-active-customers', 2, -0.10::numeric),
    ('hypothetical-retail-active-customers', 3,  0.15::numeric),
    ('hypothetical-retail-active-customers', 4, -0.25::numeric)
),
validated AS (
  SELECT
    segment,
    period_number,
    period_rate,
    1 + period_rate AS factor,
    CASE WHEN period_rate < -1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS invalid_below_minus_100,
    CASE WHEN period_rate = -1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS has_zero_factor
  FROM monthly_growth
)
SELECT
  segment,
  COUNT(*) AS n_periods,
  AVG(period_rate) AS arithmetic_mean_rate,
  CASE
    WHEN SUM(invalid_below_minus_100) > 0 THEN NULL
    WHEN SUM(has_zero_factor) > 0 THEN -1::numeric
    ELSE EXP(AVG(LN(factor))) - 1
  END AS geometric_mean_rate,
  CASE
    WHEN SUM(invalid_below_minus_100) > 0 THEN NULL
    WHEN SUM(has_zero_factor) > 0 THEN -1::numeric
    ELSE EXP(SUM(LN(factor))) - 1
  END AS cumulative_growth_rate
FROM validated
GROUP BY segment;

sections.heading: A practical diagnostic before averaging rates
paragraphs: Before approving an average percentage in a metric definition, ask what operation the average is supposed to preserve. If the result must reconcile a starting value to an ending value over multiple periods, an arithmetic average of rates is suspect. Recreate the end value from the proposed average. If the reconstruction fails, the metric label should not claim compounded growth.

Next, identify the denominator. Many percentage metrics are ratios, not growth rates. Conversion rate, defect rate, refund rate, and cancellation rate usually combine through their denominators for a reporting period. Averaging store-level or campaign-level percentages without weights is a common error, but the fix is usually total numerator divided by total denominator, not a geometric mean.

Then check the domain. Geometric means require nonnegative values in their basic product form and positive values in the log-sum implementation. For growth factors, that means each factor must be greater than or equal to zero conceptually, and greater than zero when applying ln. A factor of zero represents total loss over the remaining sequence. A factor below zero usually means the metric is not a valid compounded growth measure.

Finally, name the statistic precisely. Cumulative growth, equivalent monthly growth, arithmetic average monthly change, and average observed rate are different terms. A semantic layer can expose more than one of them, but the definitions should say which one reconciles to the start and end values. The geometric mean is useful because it makes that reconciliation explicit.
bullets: Reconstruction test: start_value times the product of factors should equal end_value, within the rounding policy of the model.
Equivalent-rate test: start_value times one plus the geometric mean rate, raised to n periods, should equal the same end value.
Weighting test: if observations are parallel groups in one period, verify whether numerator and denominator totals are available before averaging percentages.
Domain test: reject rates below negative 100% for nonnegative compounded quantities and special-case rates equal to negative 100%.

takeaways: Arithmetic averages preserve sums; compounded growth is governed by products of growth factors.
For sequential percentage changes, calculate cumulative growth as product(1 + rate) minus 1, and equivalent per-period growth as product(1 + rate)^(1/n) minus 1.
A geometric mean is not a universal fix for percentage metrics. Parallel ratios usually need denominator-weighted arithmetic aggregation.
Validate the domain before using logarithms: factors must be positive for log-sum calculations, and zero factors require explicit handling.

title: Logarithmic scales in operational metrics
description: A practical guide to using log-style transformations for operational metrics while preserving zero, negative, and signed values instead of filtering them away.
lead: Logarithmic scales are useful when a metric varies by multiplication rather than addition: 10, 100, and 1,000 are evenly spaced because each step is a tenfold change. The trap is that many operational metrics are not strictly positive. Counts can be zero. Net values, adjustments, margin, balance changes, and forecast errors can be negative. If a dashboard silently filters those rows before applying a logarithm, it can turn an operational warning into an apparently clean trend. The practical rule is simple: aggregate in the metric’s natural units first, then choose a display transform that makes zero and sign behavior explicit.

sections.heading: Why ordinary logs break operational data
paragraphs: A plain logarithm answers a narrow question: how many multiplicative steps separate positive values? On a base-10 log scale, 1, 10, 100, and 1,000 are evenly spaced. That is useful for operational metrics with long right tails, such as request volume by endpoint, item demand by SKU, or batch duration by job type, when the measured value is strictly greater than zero.

The limitation is mathematical, not cosmetic. log(x) is undefined for x = 0 and for negative x in ordinary real-valued analysis. A charting tool, SQL expression, or notebook therefore has to do something when it sees zero or negative observations. Common choices are to drop those rows, replace zero with a small constant, take the absolute value, or use a signed transformation. Only the last of those preserves the fact that the original data contained a zero or a sign.

Operational data contains these cases often. A store-day can have zero returns. A customer cohort can have negative net revenue after refunds. An inventory adjustment can be positive after a recount or negative after shrinkage. A forecast error is signed by design. These values are not dirty just because they are inconvenient for a logarithm.

This is also why the transform should not be treated as the metric definition. Measures of scale summarize variation, but the scale used for explanation is separate from the business quantity being measured. Store the natural unit, compute totals and rates according to the metric definition, and then transform a copy for inspection or display.

sections.heading: Counterexample: filtering positives changes the answer
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail operations table with one row per region. The metric is daily net order change against plan. Positive values mean more orders than planned, negative values mean fewer orders than planned, and zero means plan was met exactly.

The five observed values are: +100, +10, 0, -10, and -100 orders. In natural units, the sum is 0 and the arithmetic mean is 0. This is a balanced day: two regions are above plan, two are below plan by matching magnitudes, and one is exactly on plan.

Now suppose an analyst wants to explain the multiplicative spread and applies log10 only where the value is positive. The remaining values are +10 and +100. Their log10 values are 1 and 2. The average transformed value is 1.5, and converting that back gives 10^1.5, or about 31.62. That number is the geometric center of the positive observations only. It is not the typical region, not the average net change, and not evidence that the business was above plan.

Another attempted fix is to take log10(abs(x) + 1). This keeps every row, but it discards the sign. The transformed values are approximately 2.004, 1.041, 0, 1.041, and 2.004. The average transformed value is approximately 1.218, and converting back gives about 15.52 after subtracting 1. The problem is worse than before: the display now says there was sizable activity, but it has erased whether that activity was favorable or unfavorable.

A better display transform for this example is a signed log-style transform: signed_log10(x) = sign(x) times log10(1 + abs(x)). The transformed values are approximately +2.004, +1.041, 0, -1.041, and -2.004. Zero remains zero. Positive and negative values stay on opposite sides of the axis. Equal magnitudes with opposite signs cancel visually around the center.

That does not make the signed transform an aggregation rule. It is a display rule. If the question is total net order change, the answer is still computed in orders: +100 + 10 + 0 - 10 - 100 = 0. If the question is signed multiplicative variation, the signed transform is a reasonable way to show that the magnitude ranges from 10-order differences to 100-order differences without pretending negative values do not exist.

sections.heading: Calculation rules for practitioners
paragraphs: A useful implementation starts by classifying the metric’s valid domain. This is a modeling decision, not a visualization preference. The same numeric value can have different meanings depending on the metric: zero orders is a valid count, zero latency may indicate instrumentation behavior, and zero net revenue may be a real outcome after refunds.

Use a plain logarithm only when all valid observations are strictly positive and a multiplicative interpretation is intended. Examples can include positive-only quantities such as nonzero elapsed time or positive demand among products that had at least one sale, provided the exclusion is part of the question. The label should say what was excluded, such as “log scale, positive demand days only.”

Use a log1p-style transform for nonnegative metrics when zero is valid and the purpose is visual compression. log(1 + x) maps zero to zero and compresses large values. The tradeoff is that small values no longer have the same pure ratio interpretation as a plain logarithm. The distance between 0 and 1 is not a ratio of zero to one; it is an artifact of the plus-one transform.

Use a signed log-style transform when the metric is signed and magnitude matters. sign(x) times log(1 + abs(x)) is easy to explain: keep the sign, compress the magnitude, and leave zero at zero. This is appropriate for signed deltas, forecast errors, inventory adjustments, and net operational values. The tradeoff is that ratios across zero are not meaningful. Moving from -10 to +10 is a sign change, not a twofold increase.

Never aggregate transformed values unless the transformed quantity is the metric being analyzed. For operational reporting, this usually means totals, counts, and numerator-denominator ratios should be calculated before any log transform is applied. Transforming first and summing later changes the question.

For exact decimal quantities where rounding error would be misleading, use an appropriate exact numeric representation rather than binary floating point. PostgreSQL’s numeric type is designed for exact decimal arithmetic, with precision and scale choices made in the schema. This is separate from the log-scale question, but it matters because a clean transform cannot repair an imprecise base metric.
bullets: Classify the valid domain first: positive-only, nonnegative, or signed.
Compute business aggregates in natural units before applying any display transform.
Label the transform explicitly: log10(x), log10(1 + x), or signed log10(1 + abs(x)).
Do not hide excluded rows. Count and report zeros and negatives when a plain log is used.

sections.heading: Diagnostic query before a log scale
paragraphs: Before putting a metric on a log scale, run a domain diagnostic. The goal is not to prove that the chart will look good. The goal is to discover whether a plain logarithm would exclude valid operational states.

The following is an illustrative PostgreSQL 18-style query for a table named metric_observations. It uses ordinary aggregate checks to count positive, zero, and negative observations. Execution is not implied; adapt column names, data types, and filters to the actual model.

If negative_count is greater than zero, a plain log scale is not valid for the full metric. If zero_count is greater than zero, a plain log scale will omit or special-case valid observations. If both are zero, a plain log scale may be suitable, but only if the metric definition supports multiplicative interpretation.

codeExamples.code:
select
    metric_name,
    count(*) as row_count,
    sum(case when observed_value > 0 then 1 else 0 end) as positive_count,
    sum(case when observed_value = 0 then 1 else 0 end) as zero_count,
    sum(case when observed_value < 0 then 1 else 0 end) as negative_count,
    min(observed_value) as min_observed_value,
    max(observed_value) as max_observed_value,
    sum(observed_value) as natural_unit_sum,
    avg(observed_value) as natural_unit_average
from metric_observations
group by metric_name
order by metric_name;

sections.heading: Worked display fixture
paragraphs: Here is the same hypothetical retail fixture expressed as a small calculation table. The values are in orders. The signed display transform is shown to three decimals using base 10.

Region A has +100 orders versus plan, so signed_log10 is +log10(101), approximately +2.004. Region B has +10, so the value is +log10(11), approximately +1.041. Region C has 0, so the value is 0. Region D has -10, so the value is -log10(11), approximately -1.041. Region E has -100, so the value is -log10(101), approximately -2.004.

The transformed values are useful for visual comparison because they show two facts at once: Region A and Region E have similar magnitude, and they point in opposite operational directions. A plain log of positives would show only Region A and Region B. An absolute-value log would show large movement but erase whether it was above or below plan.

The interpretation to write beside such a chart is not “average log order change.” A clearer caption is: “Net order change versus plan, displayed with a signed log10(1 + abs(x)) scale so that zero and negative values remain visible.” That caption tells readers exactly which arithmetic is business logic and which arithmetic is presentation.

sections.heading: Tradeoffs and labeling
paragraphs: A log-style display is valuable when a linear chart would collapse most observations near the axis. It is not valuable when the transform becomes a way to avoid explaining the metric’s domain. Zero and negative values often carry the operational signal: no sales, refund-heavy cohorts, negative inventory adjustments, missed forecasts, or failed jobs with no completed records.

There is also a naming risk. Calling every compressed axis a “log scale” is imprecise. A plain log scale, a log1p transform, and a signed log transform have different meanings. The difference matters when someone tries to compare two dashboards or reproduce a metric in SQL.

A practical dashboard can expose both views. Show the natural-unit total or rate as the headline number. Use the transformed plot to explain distribution, outliers, or multiplicative spread. Include a small diagnostic count for rows that were zero or negative if the visualization uses a positive-only log scale. This prevents the visual convenience from becoming a hidden data-quality filter.

The final test is whether a reader can reconstruct the decision rule. If the metric is strictly positive, state that. If zero is valid, state how zero is displayed. If negative values are valid, preserve the sign or choose a different chart. The point of logarithmic scales in operational metrics is not to make the data look smoother; it is to explain large relative differences without losing the states that operations teams need to see.

takeaways: A plain logarithm is only valid for strictly positive values; zeros and negatives require an explicit modeling decision.
Filtering to positive rows can change the operational answer, not just the chart appearance.
Use signed log-style transforms for signed metrics when the goal is to display multiplicative magnitude while preserving zero and sign.
Aggregate in natural units first, then transform for display or diagnosis.
